Cutting Food Cost: Inventory Habits That Protect Your Margin
Control food cost in your Nepali cafe with better inventory habits — tracking stock, spotting waste and theft, par levels, recipe costing, and low-stock alerts.

Food cost is where cafe profits quietly disappear. You can be busy, well-reviewed, and full every evening, and still barely break even because too much of what you buy ends up in the bin, walks out the back door, or gets served without ever being charged. The good news is that food cost is one of the most controllable numbers in your business — not through one big change, but through a handful of steady habits.

## Know your food cost percentage

Food cost percentage is simply the cost of ingredients divided by the sales they generate, as a percentage. If a coffee costs you Rs 40 in beans, milk, and cup and you sell it for Rs 160, that item runs at 25%. Cafes and restaurants generally aim to keep overall food cost within a target range — where exactly depends on your concept and pricing.

You cannot manage what you do not measure. Before optimising anything, work out your current food cost for a full month: opening stock value, plus purchases, minus closing stock, gives you what you actually consumed. Compare that to sales. The gap between what you *should* have used (based on what you sold) and what you *actually* used is your waste, theft, and error — and that gap is where the money is.

## Track stock like it is cash

Inventory is cash sitting on your shelves. Treat it that way.

- **Do a physical count on a fixed schedule.** Weekly for most items, more often for high-value or fast-moving ones like meat, cheese, and coffee. Pick a time — usually close or open — and stick to it.
- **Count in consistent units.** Decide whether milk is in litres or packets and never mix. Inconsistent units are the single biggest cause of counts that never reconcile.
- **Value your stock.** A count of "12 bags of coffee" means little; "12 bags at Rs 1,200 = Rs 14,400" tells you what is tied up on the shelf.

A POS like GoServe can deduct ingredients from stock as items sell and flag when a count drifts from what sales predict, which turns the weekly count from a guessing game into a quick check against a known expected figure.

### Set par levels

A par level is the minimum quantity of an item you want on hand before you reorder. Setting pars stops both problems at once: running out of your best-seller mid-service, and over-ordering perishables that spoil before you use them.

Set pars based on how fast something moves and how long delivery takes. Coffee beans with a reliable weekly supplier need a different par than fresh milk you buy daily. Review pars before festival season — your Dashain and Tihar demand will not match a quiet monsoon week.

## Spot waste and theft

Waste and theft look identical on a spreadsheet: stock that left without a matching sale. You separate them by watching where it happens.

**Waste** usually shows up as:

- Perishables spoiling before use — a sign your pars are too high or your rotation is poor.
- Over-portioning — a barista free-pouring milk, a cook heaping plates beyond spec.
- Prep mistakes and burnt batches that never get logged.

**Theft or leakage** shows up as:

- Stock disappearing with no waste log and no sale — cash sales not rung up, drinks given to friends off the books, product walking out the back.
- A stubborn gap between expected and actual usage that does not track with any waste you can see.

The defence against both is the same: log everything. Log wastage when you throw something out. Log staff meals and comps. Log the coffee you pulled to re-dial the grinder. Once every legitimate reason a unit can leave is written down, whatever remains in the gap is the problem you need to chase.

> If stock can leave your cafe without leaving a record, you do not have an inventory problem — you have a recording problem, and it will always look like theft even when it is only mess.

## Cost your recipes

You cannot price well or spot a problem item without knowing what each dish costs to make. Recipe costing means breaking a menu item down to its ingredients and their cost.

Take your best-selling latte: espresso (beans), milk, cup, lid, and a share of syrup if flavoured. Add it up and you have the true cost. Do this for every item and two things become obvious — which items make you real money and which are barely worth making. When a supplier raises the price of milk, recipe costing tells you instantly which menu prices need to move and by how much, instead of guessing.

Recipe costing also disciplines portions. Once the kitchen knows a dish is built to a spec that costs Rs X, over-portioning becomes visible rather than invisible.

## Use low-stock alerts

The old way is to notice you are out when a customer orders it. The better way is a low-stock alert that fires when an item drops to its par level, so you reorder before you run dry. This matters most for items that anchor your menu — running out of coffee in a coffee shop is not a small mistake. Software that tracks stock against sales can flag low items automatically; if you are on pen and paper, a simple reorder board by the store cupboard works too, as long as someone owns it.

## Keep your suppliers disciplined

A surprising amount of food cost leaks in at the receiving door.

- **Check every delivery against the order and the bill.** Weigh what should be weighed. Suppliers make mistakes — some honest, some not — and if you sign without checking, you pay for what you did not get.
- **Keep supplier bills.** They are your purchase record for both cost tracking and VAT input claims. See our note on [VAT and compliant billing](/blog/vat-ird-billing-for-restaurants) for why purchase records matter at tax time.
- **Track price changes.** When a supplier's price moves, it should trigger a look at your recipe cost and menu price, not just quiet acceptance.
- **Do not over-rely on one supplier for critical items.** A single delivery falling through the week before Tihar is the kind of thing that ruins a rush.

## Small habits, protected margin

None of this is complicated. Count on a schedule, value your stock, set pars, log every reason product leaves, cost your recipes, react to low-stock alerts, and check what your suppliers deliver. Each habit is minor on its own; together they close the gap between what you buy and what you sell — and that gap is your profit.

Food cost control is not a one-time project. It is a rhythm you build into the week, the same way you build the [opening and closing routines](/blog/running-a-cafe-in-nepal) that keep the rest of the cafe running.

QR Menus for Cafes in Nepal: Why and How to Set One Up
A practical guide to QR menus for Nepali cafes — faster ordering, instant updates, no reprinting, and how to pair a QR menu with eSewa and Khalti payments.

Walk into almost any busy cafe in Kathmandu now and you will spot a little QR sticker on the table. QR menus went from novelty to normal in a few short years, and for good reason — they solve real problems that laminated menus never could. If you are still reprinting menus every time a supplier price moves, here is why a QR menu is worth setting up and how to roll one out without frustrating your customers.

## Why a QR menu earns its place

### It kills reprinting costs and delays

Every price change, every new seasonal drink, every item you run out of used to mean either reprinting the whole menu or crossing things out with a pen. With a QR menu you edit once and every table sees the update instantly. When your milk supplier raises prices before Dashain, you adjust the menu that morning instead of living with old prices for weeks because reprinting felt like too much hassle.

### It speeds up ordering

Customers can look at the menu the moment they sit down, without waiting for a server to bring one and come back. On a busy evening that head start on decisions moves your whole floor faster. It also frees your staff from ferrying menus around so they can focus on making and serving.

### It keeps the menu honest

A QR menu that is connected to your POS can hide items that are out of stock automatically, so nobody orders the momo you sold out of an hour ago. That single feature prevents a lot of small disappointments.

### It works alongside your printed menu

QR menus are not all-or-nothing. Plenty of Nepali cafes keep a few printed menus for older customers or for tables that prefer paper, and let everyone else scan. The QR is an addition, not a replacement — offer both and let people choose.

## How to roll one out

Setting up a QR menu is more about doing a few things carefully than about anything technical.

1. **Get your menu into a clean digital form first.** Categories, item names, prices, and a short description where it helps. This is the foundation — a messy menu online is worse than a tidy one on paper.
2. **Decide how prices are shown.** Be consistent about whether prices include VAT and service charge. Surprises at the bottom of the bill sour the experience; see our note on [VAT and compliant billing](/blog/vat-ird-billing-for-restaurants) for how to present this cleanly.
3. **Generate one QR per table or one for the whole cafe.** A single QR on a standee at the counter works for smaller places. Per-table QR codes matter more if you want table-linked ordering later.
4. **Print the QR clearly and place it well.** A crisp, well-lit sticker at a comfortable reading angle. Add a one-line prompt like "Scan for menu" in both Nepali and English.
5. **Test it yourself on a cheap phone and slow data.** Not everyone is on fast wifi. If your menu takes ten seconds to load on a modest phone over mobile data, trim it down.

A POS like GoServe generates a QR menu straight from the menu you already manage for billing, so there is no second system to keep in sync — you update the menu once and both your bills and your QR reflect it.

## Keeping it current is the whole point

The failure mode of QR menus is neglect. A QR that opens a menu with last season's prices and three sold-out items is worse than paper, because customers assume digital means accurate.

- **Update stock status daily.** Mark out-of-stock items so they disappear or grey out.
- **Change prices the day they change,** not at the end of the month.
- **Retire seasonal items** when the season ends. A pumpkin-spice anything lingering into spring looks careless.
- **Check the link weekly.** Scan your own QR once a week to confirm it loads fast and shows what you expect.

> A QR menu is a promise that what customers see is what they can actually get. Keep that promise and it builds trust; break it and it erodes trust faster than a paper menu ever could.

## Pair it with eSewa and Khalti

The natural companion to a QR menu is a QR payment. Once a customer is comfortable scanning to see the menu, scanning to pay through eSewa or Khalti feels like the same motion. A few practical tips:

- **Keep your payment QR separate and clearly labelled.** Do not let customers confuse the menu QR with the payment QR. Different stickers, different spots, clear labels.
- **Confirm payment on your own screen** before clearing the table. A screenshot of a "sent" message is not confirmation — the money landing in your account is.
- **Record the payment method on the bill.** Whether it was cash, eSewa, or Khalti, tagging it as you go is what makes your [end-of-day reconciliation](/blog/closing-the-day-shift-reconciliation) match up cleanly.

Digital payments also leave a clean record, which makes your daily close and your tax reporting simpler. The QR menu gets the order in faster; the QR payment gets the money in cleaner. Together they take real friction out of a busy service.

## Start small and grow into it

You do not need to digitise everything at once. Start with one well-made QR menu at the counter, keep a few printed copies for those who want them, and commit to updating stock and prices daily. Once that habit sticks, you can layer on table-linked ordering and tighter payment integration.

A QR menu is one of the cheapest upgrades a Nepali cafe can make, and one of the few that pays back immediately in saved printing, faster tables, and fewer "sorry, we are out of that" moments.

Closing the Day: Shift Reconciliation for Nepali Cafes
A step-by-step end-of-day close for cafes in Nepal — counting the drawer, matching cash and eSewa/Khalti to sales, handling discrepancies, and why it protects owners.

The last ten minutes of the day decide whether you actually know how your cafe is doing. A proper end-of-day close — counting the drawer, matching every rupee of cash and digital payment against sales, and resolving any gap — is the single most protective habit an owner can build. Skip it and small leaks go unnoticed for months. Do it every night and problems surface while they are still small enough to fix.

## Why the close protects you

When you are not on the floor every hour, the daily close is how you keep watch without hovering. It does three things at once:

- **It catches leakage early.** A drawer that comes up short two nights in a row is a signal you can act on now, not a mystery you discover in a quarterly panic.
- **It keeps your numbers honest.** Your recorded sales, your cash, and your digital receipts should all tell the same story. When they do, your books are trustworthy — for you and for the [IRD](/blog/vat-ird-billing-for-restaurants).
- **It builds a culture of accountability.** When staff know the drawer is counted every night, casual "borrowing" and sloppy change-making mostly stop on their own.

> A discrepancy is not an accusation. It is information. The point of the close is to surface it while you can still explain it.

## The close, step by step

Run the same sequence every night. Consistency is what makes the numbers comparable from day to day.

### 1. Stop and cut off

Settle any open tables and stop taking new orders on the till you are closing. You cannot reconcile a drawer that is still moving. If you run late tables, close the shift and start a fresh count for the after-hours service.

### 2. Pull your sales total by payment method

Before you touch the cash, get your sales figure broken down: how much was cash, how much eSewa, how much Khalti, how much card or bank transfer. This is the target your counts must hit. If you tagged payment method on every bill during service — as you should — this is a single report. A POS like GoServe produces this split at the tap of a button, which is what makes the rest of the close fast.

### 3. Count the drawer

Count the physical cash carefully.

- Count notes and coins and write down the total.
- **Subtract the opening float** (the cash you started the day with — say Rs 3,000). What remains is your cash sales for the day.
- **Add back any cash paid out of the drawer** during the day — a supplier paid in cash, petty expenses — because that money left as expense, not as missing cash. Keep the chits.

Your adjusted cash figure should match the cash sales from your sales report.

### 4. Match the digital payments

For eSewa and Khalti, confirm the received amounts against your own account records, not against customer screenshots. Add up what actually landed and compare to the eSewa and Khalti totals on your sales report. Do the same for card and bank transfers. Each method should reconcile on its own — this is why tagging the method per bill matters so much.

### 5. Note the result

Write down the outcome for each method: matched, short, or over, and by how much. A close that is exactly zero every single night is nice, but small variances happen. What matters is that you record them and watch the pattern.

## Handling discrepancies

When something does not match, resolve it calmly and methodically.

1. **Recount first.** Most discrepancies are counting errors or the float being added or subtracted wrong.
2. **Check for untagged or miscategorised payments.** A cash sale accidentally marked as eSewa will make one short and the other over by the same amount — a classic offsetting pair that points straight at the fix.
3. **Look for unlogged payouts and comps.** Cash paid to a supplier without a chit, or a free drink never recorded, both look like a shortage.
4. **Check your digital confirmations.** A payment the customer "sent" that never actually arrived is a real loss, not a counting error — and worth catching the same night.
5. **Log it either way.** If you cannot explain a small gap, still record it. A patterns of Rs 50 shortages tells you more over a month than any single night does.

Set a threshold for what counts as normal. A few rupees of rounding is noise. A consistent shortage, or one large gap, deserves a real conversation.

## Make it a fixed routine

The close only protects you if it happens the same way every night, even — especially — when it was busy.

- **Same person, same time, same order of steps.** Assign who closes so it is never "someone will do it".
- **Keep the opening float constant.** A fixed float (and counting it at open) is what makes the close subtractable. A random starting amount makes every close guesswork.
- **Keep the chits.** Every cash payout needs a slip. No slip, no deduction — it just reads as missing money.
- **Do it before the fatigue.** Close while you can still think, not at 1am when every number blurs.

This close mirrors the [opening routine](/blog/running-a-cafe-in-nepal) — a known float at open, a matched count at close. The two bookend your day and keep the cash story unbroken.

## The payoff

A cafe that closes its books every night runs with a quiet confidence a cafe that does not simply cannot have. You know your real daily sales. You know cash and digital match. You catch leaks in days, not quarters. And when tax time comes, your records already agree with your takings, so there is nothing to reconstruct or explain.

Ten minutes a night is a small price for knowing exactly where your money is. Build the habit, keep it consistent, and let the numbers do the watching for you.

  3. Look for unlogged payouts and comps. Cash paid to a supplier without a chit, or a free drink never recorded, both look like a shortage.
  4. Check your digital confirmations. A payment the customer “sent” that never actually arrived is a real loss, not a counting error — and worth catching the same night.
  5. Log it either way. If you cannot explain a small gap, still record it. A patterns of Rs 50 shortages tells you more over a month than any single night does.

Set a threshold for what counts as normal. A few rupees of rounding is noise. A consistent shortage, or one large gap, deserves a real conversation.

Make it a fixed routine

The close only protects you if it happens the same way every night, even — especially — when it was busy.

  • Same person, same time, same order of steps. Assign who closes so it is never “someone will do it”.
  • Keep the opening float constant. A fixed float (and counting it at open) is what makes the close subtractable. A random starting amount makes every close guesswork.
  • Keep the chits. Every cash payout needs a slip. No slip, no deduction — it just reads as missing money.
  • Do it before the fatigue. Close while you can still think, not at 1am when every number blurs.

This close mirrors the opening routine — a known float at open, a matched count at close. The two bookend your day and keep the cash story unbroken.

The payoff

A cafe that closes its books every night runs with a quiet confidence a cafe that does not simply cannot have. You know your real daily sales. You know cash and digital match. You catch leaks in days, not quarters. And when tax time comes, your records already agree with your takings, so there is nothing to reconstruct or explain.

Ten minutes a night is a small price for knowing exactly where your money is. Build the habit, keep it consistent, and let the numbers do the watching for you.

VAT and IRD-Compliant Billing for Nepali Restaurants
How 13% VAT and IRD billing rules work for cafes and restaurants in Nepal — when VAT applies, what a compliant bill shows, service charge, and common pitfalls.

Billing is where a lot of Nepali restaurants get nervous, and understandably so. Between VAT, service charge, and what the Inland Revenue Department (IRD) expects to see on a bill, it is easy to either overcomplicate things or quietly cut corners that come back to bite you at audit time. This is a plain-language walkthrough of how VAT and compliant billing generally work for cafes and restaurants in Nepal.

A note before we start: tax rules and thresholds change, and your exact obligations depend on your registration, turnover, and location. Treat everything here as a working overview, not legal advice. Confirm the current rules and your specific position with a qualified accountant or directly with the IRD.

## VAT and PAN: which one are you?

Every business needs a PAN (Permanent Account Number). Whether you also need to register for VAT depends mainly on your turnover and the nature of your business.

- **PAN-only (small taxpayer):** many small cafes operate under PAN without charging VAT, often paying tax under a turnover-based or presumptive scheme.
- **VAT-registered:** once you cross the registration threshold — or if you choose to register — you charge 13% VAT on taxable sales, file VAT returns, and can claim VAT paid on your purchases.

The threshold and the exact schemes are the kind of thing that gets revised, so this is precisely the point to confirm with your accountant. Registering for VAT when you do not need to, or failing to register when you should have, both cause avoidable headaches.

## When 13% VAT applies

If you are VAT-registered, VAT applies to your taxable sales — for a restaurant, that is essentially the food and drink you sell. The standard rate in Nepal is **13%**. The key questions in practice are *how* you present it and *whether it is included or added on top*.

There are two common approaches:

1. **VAT-inclusive pricing** — your menu price already contains the 13%. A Rs 226 coffee is Rs 200 plus Rs 26 VAT. The customer sees a round menu price; the bill breaks out the VAT portion.
2. **VAT-exclusive pricing** — your menu shows Rs 200 and the 13% is added as a separate line at the bottom.

Both are used in Nepal. Inclusive pricing tends to feel friendlier to customers because the shelf price is the price they pay; exclusive pricing makes the tax explicit. Whichever you pick, be consistent and make sure the maths on the printed bill is correct and clearly labelled.

## Service charge is not VAT

This trips up owners and customers alike. **Service charge and VAT are two different things.**

- **Service charge** is a charge the restaurant adds for service, commonly **10%**. It is your revenue (typically pooled and distributed to staff, subject to labour rules). It is not a government tax.
- **VAT** is a government tax at 13% that you collect on behalf of the state and remit to the IRD.

The order of calculation matters and should be consistent. A widely used sequence is:

1. Subtotal of items — say Rs 1,000
2. Add service charge at 10% — Rs 100, giving Rs 1,100
3. Add VAT at 13% on that amount — Rs 143, giving a total of Rs 1,243

Whether VAT is calculated before or after service charge, and exactly how service charge is treated, is something to nail down with your accountant so every bill you print is defensible. The important thing for the customer's trust is that each line is labelled and adds up.

## What an IRD-compliant bill should show

A compliant tax invoice is not just a total scribbled on a pad. As a general expectation, a VAT bill should clearly show:

- Your **business name, address, and PAN/VAT number**
- A **unique, sequential invoice number** and the date
- A **line for each item** with quantity and price
- The **subtotal**, any **service charge**, and the **VAT amount shown separately**
- The **grand total**

Sequential invoice numbering matters. Bills should run in an unbroken sequence, and you should not be able to quietly delete one from the middle. If a sale is voided or refunded, that should be recorded as a void or credit — not by making the original bill vanish. Some businesses in Nepal are also required to use IRD-approved or registered billing software with specific controls; whether that applies to you depends on your category and turnover, so check.

> The simplest test: could you hand any bill from any day to an auditor and have the sequence, the maths, and the tax lines all make sense? If yes, you are in good shape.

This is one of the strongest reasons to bill on software rather than a pad. A POS like GoServe keeps invoice numbers sequential, records voids instead of hiding them, and prints a clean bill with your PAN, itemised lines, service charge, and VAT laid out the way an auditor expects — which turns tax time from a scramble into a report you can just export.

## Keep records you can actually produce

Compliance is not only about the bill you hand the customer — it is about the trail behind it.

- Keep your **sales records** (all invoices, in sequence) and your **purchase records** (bills from suppliers, ideally with their VAT invoices so you can claim input VAT).
- File your **VAT returns on time**. Late filing attracts penalties, and they add up.
- Reconcile daily so your recorded sales match your actual cash and digital takings. If your books say one thing and your [end-of-day count](/blog/closing-the-day-shift-reconciliation) says another, fix it while you still remember why.
- Hold on to records for the retention period the law requires — again, confirm the current duration.

## Common pitfalls

- **Charging VAT without being registered.** If you print "VAT 13%" on bills but are not a VAT-registered business, you are collecting a tax you are not authorised to collect. Do not do this.
- **Hiding sales to reduce tax.** Under-reporting cash sales is common and genuinely risky. Digital payments through eSewa, Khalti, and banks leave a trail regardless, so a gap between your digital receipts and your declared sales is exactly what draws scrutiny.
- **Confusing customers with unlabelled charges.** A total that is mysteriously higher than the menu prices, with no breakdown, reads as a scam even when it is honest. Label every line.
- **Breaking the invoice sequence.** Gaps and deletions in your bill numbers are a red flag. Void properly instead.
- **Assuming last year's rules still apply.** Rates, thresholds, and software requirements get updated. Build a yearly habit of checking with your accountant.

## Keep it clean and it stays simple

Compliant billing is not about being clever — it is about being consistent and transparent. Decide how you present VAT and service charge, print bills that show every line clearly with your PAN and a sequential number, keep both your sales and purchase records, and file on time. Do that and an IRD review becomes a formality rather than a crisis.

Running a Cafe in Nepal: A Practical Daily Operations Checklist
A hands-on guide to running a cafe in Nepal day to day — opening and closing routines, table flow, staff roles, handling the rush, and cash versus digital.

Running a cafe in Nepal is a game of small, repeated habits. The espresso machine, the seating, and the menu matter, but what actually keeps a place profitable is how consistently the same routines get done every single day — whether you are open in Thamel, Pokhara Lakeside, or a quiet neighbourhood in Lalitpur. This is a practical checklist you can adapt to your own floor.

## Start the day with a clean open

The first hour sets the tone for everything after it. A rushed open leads to a rushed lunch. Build a fixed opening routine and make it non-negotiable.

- **Count the drawer** before the first order. Write down the opening float (for example Rs 3,000 in small notes and coins) so you have a known starting point for the evening count.
- **Check power and backup.** Load-shedding is less brutal than it used to be, but it still happens. Confirm your inverter or backup is charged, and know which appliances you can and cannot run on backup at once.
- **Test wifi and your payment QR.** Print or wipe down your eSewa and Khalti QR standee. A smudged or peeling QR loses you sales at the counter.
- **Prep and taste.** Check milk, syrups, and anything perishable. Smell the milk before you trust the date on it. Do a quick tasting shot on the espresso machine and dial in the grind.
- **Brief the team.** Thirty seconds is enough: what is 86'd (out of stock), any specials, any large bookings, and who is on which station.

### Set your stations

Even a small cafe runs better when everyone knows their zone. A typical split:

- **Counter / cashier** — takes orders, handles billing and payments, owns the drawer.
- **Barista / kitchen** — makes drinks and food, calls out when something runs low.
- **Floor** — clears tables, refills water, reads the room for who needs the bill.

In a two-person cafe one person wears two hats, but the roles should still be spoken out loud so nothing falls through the cracks.

## Keep order flow tight

Most cafe chaos comes from orders getting lost between the table and the kitchen. Slips of paper go missing, verbal orders get forgotten, and the customer who ordered first gets served last.

A clear ticket flow fixes this. Every order should move through the same path: taken, sent to the kitchen, made, served, and settled. When a table can see their order was heard and is moving, complaints drop sharply. A POS like GoServe keeps each table's running order in one place and sends tickets straight to the kitchen screen, so nothing depends on a barista remembering table 4 wanted oat milk. If you run on paper, at least use numbered dockets and a spike so the sequence is never in doubt.

### Table numbering that survives a rush

Number or name every table and stick to it. During Dashain and Tihar season your floor will be full and half your staff may be new hires covering the rush. A consistent table map is what lets a new server drop the right bill at the right table without asking around.

## Handle the rush without losing the plot

Peak hours — the morning coffee wave, the lunch crowd, and the long evening sit-downs — are where money is made and where mistakes multiply. A few things that hold up under pressure:

1. **Take payment method early on busy tables.** Knowing a table will pay by QR versus cash lets you settle faster when they stand up to leave.
2. **Batch, don't scatter.** Fire similar drinks together. Making four Americanos in one go beats making them one at a time between other tickets.
3. **Keep the counter clear.** A pile of unsettled bills at the till is how money and orders go missing. Close each table as it leaves.
4. **Watch your 86 list.** The fastest way to anger a full house is to take an order for something you ran out of an hour ago. Update the out-of-stock list the moment something runs dry.

> The busiest hour is the one where your routines have to run themselves. If a step only works when things are calm, it is not a routine yet.

## Cash versus digital

Nepal has moved fast to digital payments, and most cafes now see a healthy mix of cash, eSewa, and Khalti — plus the occasional card or bank transfer. Handle each cleanly:

- **Cash** goes straight into the drawer, change comes straight back out. Do not let staff make change from their pockets; it wrecks your count.
- **eSewa / Khalti** should be confirmed on your own screen before you clear the table. "I already sent it, didi" is not a confirmation — the transaction landing in your account is.
- **Record the method on every bill.** At the end of the night your drawer cash plus your digital receipts must match your total sales. If you do not tag the payment method as you go, reconciling later is guesswork. We cover this in detail in [closing the day](/blog/closing-the-day-shift-reconciliation).

If you are still deciding how to present your menu and take orders, a [QR menu](/blog/qr-menus-for-cafes) pairs naturally with digital payment and cuts the queue at your counter.

## Common mistakes that quietly cost you

- **No opening float discipline.** If the drawer starts at a random amount, your close never balances and you can never tell theft from sloppiness.
- **Free drinks that never get logged.** Staff coffees, owner's tea, a comp for a regular — all fine, but log them. Untracked giveaways look identical to shrinkage.
- **Menu prices that do not include the maths.** Decide early how you show VAT and service charge on the bill and keep it consistent. Customers forgive a fair price; they do not forgive a surprise line at the bottom.
- **Ignoring stock until you run out.** Waiting for the shelf to be empty before reordering guarantees you will be out of your best-seller on your busiest day.
- **No end-of-day count.** Skipping the close "because it was busy" is exactly when you most needed to do it.

## Close the day properly

The close mirrors the open. Count the drawer, match cash and digital to sales, note any discrepancy, restock what you can for tomorrow, and lock up knowing your numbers. Ten disciplined minutes at close saves you an hour of confusion the next morning and protects you from slow leaks that add up over a month.

Running a cafe well in Nepal is not about fancy systems — it is about doing the boring things the same way every day so your team can move fast when it counts. Get the open, the order flow, and the close right, and the rest of the business has room to grow.
